symptoms: Stage retried several times with the same failure, and the job eventually aborts
The failure names a remote block and a host, not a line of the job's own code
A stage that read fine in earlier runs starts failing as the shuffle grows
likely_causes: Executor holding the shuffle block died or was preempted, and the block went with it
Long GC pause on the block holder made the fetch time out
Too many concurrent fetch requests against one host, saturating inbound connections
diagnostic_steps: Check whether an executor was lost around the failed stage: the fact spark.executor.lost carries the removal reason
Read spark.stage.shuffle for the volume moved by the stage that failed
Read the effective values of spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries and spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight from spark.conf_effective, and treat the Spark defaults (3 and Int.MaxValue) as the baseline
fixes: Find out why the executor died before touching retry settings: a fetch failure caused by an OOM kill is a memory problem wearing a network problem's clothes
Cap spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight when the failure concentrates on one host, since the documented default is unbounded and a large cluster can saturate a node with inbound connections
Raise spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries or spark.shuffle.io.retryWait only for genuinely transient network failures, and record that the cause was diagnosed as transient
unsafe_fixes: Raising the retry count while an executor keeps dying: it converts a fast failure into a slow one and hides the reason the executor died
Setting spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight to a small arbitrary number without measuring, which serialises the fetch and slows every healthy stage as well
verification: Re-run the job and confirm the stage completes without retries, with the same input volume as the failing run
rollback: Revert the shuffle configuration overrides; they are runtime settings and change no data
